I think any currency backed on a good in the modern economy would explode. The reason is that it would be inherently deflationary. Imagine for an instance there are 100 units of gold in our economy. You have 1 unit so everybody else has 99 units to go around for their goods and services. You now earn 1 more unit, but instead of spending it you tuck it under your mattress. There are now only 98 units of gold to go around. This means that prices have deflated and one unit of gold is worth even more. To adjust for this wages end up going down and pricing in general deflates. The person who's hoarding away that 2 gold just got relatively much richer while everybody else got relatively poorer. In this sort of system the ideal strategy is wealth hoarding. Each dollar you take out of the economy makes your money worth that much more. This is very dangerous.

Our economy on the other hand has basically turned into funny money, but I think it's at least well intentioned. The idea is to make sure this exact hoarding encouraging deflation doesn't happen. So the Fed constantly jams trillions of dollars into the economy and banks are allowed to create money out of thin air in the form of debt lent on margin. All of this is trying to desperately to ensure more money keeps getting into the economy and to more generally cause inflation because inflation is the answer to wealth hoarding. If people's money loses value if they don't spend it, then they're obligated to do just that and that keeps the entire economy churning along.

And lending could in fact harm themselves if the rates they charge do not overcome their own losses incurred due to mitigating deflation. That's the reason the Fed today is freaking out about deflation and even considering doing things like setting a negative nominal reserve interest rate - literally paying banks to lend! Compare this to inflation where their reserves are literally becoming worth less every single day. If they don't invest their money dwindles away.

Beyond that banks in general would be radically different. In our current system banks are allowed to create money out of thin air. Bob deposits $100. The bank can now lend out $90 (and charge interest on that money) even if that's all the money they have. That money gets spent and deposited at another bank which now lends out $81 and the process repeats on downward. Work the math out and our system results in $100 of real money deposits injecting a $1000 of monopoly money into the economy in the form of debt. Obviously banks would not be allowed to pull money out of thin air in a goods backed economy and that would have a radical impact on our entire notion of banking. Deflation can and has destroyed economies as stapleremover mentioned. There are so many consequences that it's really difficult to enumerate them all in a single post. I'll just hit on a few:

  • Deflation means products a company sells are worth less. They're going to decrease their costs. This in theory tends to mean reduced wages. In reality reducing wages is difficult so it tends to actually mean layoffs. Layoffs in turn further decrease the amount of money circulating which can create self feedback loop into a further depressive cycle.

  • During deflation debts become more burdensome. As each unit of money becomes worth more, each unit of debt becomes worth more. We live in a debt based economy which makes this part particularly nasty. Furthermore it does not balance out. Though the amount debtors owe to creditors increases, in a deflationary economy it's unlikely the creditors will increase their spending by any comparable amount. After all each penny they spend stands to be worth even more had they not spent it. This applies to individuals as much as it does to huge banks investing on margin as it does to companies deciding whether or not take a loan for expansion.

  • Deflation ruins investment. Imagine you're invested in a company. Under deflation the valuation of that company is going to decrease as their products become worth less. How do people respond to this? They take their money out of markets and investments. That in turn decreases the valuation of those companies even further and it rapidly becomes a race to get all the money out. And we get a market crash.

And many more. You really do not want to live in an economy in depression.
